## Definition

Let $\mathcal Q$ be a family of probability laws on a common measurable sample space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)$, and let $\Sigma(Q)\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be a specified matrix parameter for each $Q\in\mathcal Q$, with fixed $p\ge1$. An estimator is a measurable map $\widehat\Sigma:(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)\to(\mathbb R^{p\times p},\mathcal B(\mathbb R^{p\times p}))$. Define its squared operator risk at $Q$ and the minimax risk over $\mathcal Q$ by
$$R_Q(\widehat\Sigma)=\mathbb E_Q\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(Q)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2,\qquad
\mathfrak R(\mathcal Q)=\inf_{\widehat\Sigma}\sup_{Q\in\mathcal Q}R_Q(\widehat\Sigma).$$

For a family $\mathcal P$ of one-observation laws on a common measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and an integer $n\ge1$, the $n$-observation experiment observes $n$ independent observations, each with law $P$. Its sample space is $(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})$ and its sample law is the finite product probability measure $P^{\otimes n}$; this is the joint law of the IID family in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and [[def-independent-random-elements]]. For estimators $\widehat\Sigma:(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})\to(\mathbb R^{p\times p},\mathcal B(\mathbb R^{p\times p}))$, define
$$R_{n,P}(\widehat\Sigma)=\mathbb E_{P^{\otimes n}}\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(P)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2,\qquad
\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal P)=\inf_{\widehat\Sigma}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}R_{n,P}(\widehat\Sigma).$$

An infinite expectation is allowed, so every measurable estimator has an extended nonnegative risk. The operator norm is from [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a positive integer $k$, take the product probability law of an independent standard normal $G$ and an independent $Q_k\sim\chi_k^2$. The **Student t law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $t_k$, is the law of
$$
T_k=\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{G}{\sqrt{Q_k/k}},&Q_k>0,\\
0,&Q_k=0.
\end{cases}
$$
For positive integers $r,s$, take independent $Q_r\sim\chi_r^2$ and $Q_s\sim\chi_s^2$. The **Fisher F law with degrees $(r,s)$**, denoted $F_{r,s}$, is the law of
$$
F_{r,s}=\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{Q_r/r}{Q_s/s},&Q_s>0,\\
0,&Q_s=0.
\end{cases}
$$
The displayed piecewise maps are Borel measurable: each quotient is continuous on its Borel positive-denominator region, and the value on the Borel zero set is constant. The positive-degree chi-square lemma proves that the denominators are positive almost surely, so these versions agree almost surely with the usual quotients. Zero degrees are excluded from both definitions.
